sections.heading: C.1 Simulated decision states
sections.text: Simulators give exact ground truth for both actions and facts, so most paired states come from three of them. In ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) we use the unseen evaluation games, plus the seen games as a separate cell; in BabyAI-Text we use BALROG’s text rendering ( Paglieri et al., 2025 ; Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2019 ; Carta et al., 2023 ) ; and in TextWorld we generate cooking games at four TALES difficulty settings ( Côté et al., 2018 ; Cui et al., 2025 ) . Trajectories are rolled out by the environment’s own expert, by a noisy variant that takes a uniformly random admissible action with probability 0.2, and by a variant that issues invalid commands. This puts failures, error feedback and detours into the traces, which successful demonstrations rarely contain. No language model takes part in the roll-outs. Gold actions use only what the trace reveals. For each state we build a map from the observations so far and compute the first actions of all shortest plans. A state is determinable when the needed objects have already been observed and the gold set is the same whether unseen cells are assumed free, assumed blocked, or taken from the true map. Otherwise it is an exploration state, whose gold is the set of actions that reveal unseen locations. Sampled items were checked against breadth-first search in the real environments; for example, 234 of 234 BabyAI items and 63 of 63 TextWorld items matched. Probe answers are read from the simulator state. On these environments we build the ladders and controls of § 2.5 . ALFWorld cells vary trace length, and a distance ladder inserts valid but irrelevant steps between the decisive observation and the decision. Observation minimal pairs move a sighting to another receptacle. Novelty cells rename objects and verbs or replace action names with opaque identifiers while keeping their descriptions. BabyAI and TextWorld cells follow the environments’ difficulty levels. Confirmation cohorts generated later from new seeds re-test the main findings on states that no earlier run had seen. Separate TextWorld cohorts change the rules of cooking in the game description, so that prior knowledge about recipes no longer applies.

sections.heading: Customer service.
sections.text: From τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench airline and retail ( Barres et al., 2026 ) we take decision states from recorded and native trajectories. Tool calls are enumerated from the task database, and probes ask about record fields and whether a policy permits an action. Minimal pairs edit one policy-relevant field so that the correct call changes, or edit an irrelevant field so that it does not. A native recovery panel places the agent after a failed or incomplete call.

sections.heading: Offline traces and tools.
sections.text: AgentRM trees supply all sibling actions at a node together with value estimates ( Xia et al., 2025 ) . Mind2Web supplies all candidate page elements and operations ( Deng et al., 2023 ) . Toucan trajectories, ToolRet, BFCL and When2Call supply tool selection over full tool lists that include tools the model has not seen, as well as the choice between calling a tool, asking the user, and abstaining ( Xu et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2025 ; Patil et al., 2025 ; Ross et al., 2025 ) . These sources have no native comprehension labels. A separate panel adds visible-field probes, whose answers are stated explicitly in the trace, to a subset of them.

sections.heading: Coding traces.
sections.text: To test feedback reading in software agents without asking the model to write code, we build 360 records from real SWE-smith repository images. Each case combines two genuine patches to different files in the same repository, runs the published tests, and asks which edit caused a named check to regress, whether the displayed evidence is current or stale, and which limited next action follows. The 50 test source pairs span 17 repositories, which are disjoint from the 11 development repositories.

sections.heading: Trace judgments.
sections.text: AgentRewardBench, R-Judge and Who&When ask for judgments about a completed trajectory, namely success, side effects, safety and the failing step ( Lù et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . We report them as a separate family, since they are not next-action decisions.

sections.heading: C.3 Text-understanding primitives
sections.text: Twenty-four task groups (32,700 test records) measure negation, multi-hop reasoning, long context with distractors, multi-turn recollection and correction, new label definitions, counterfactual rules, and logical reasoning. Each group is arranged along a difficulty ladder, for example hop count or context length. Sources include CondaQA, ScoNe, ProofWriter, CLUTRR, MuSiQue, BABILong, CLINC150, MASSIVE, CLadder and BoardgameQA, together with programmatic generators ( Ravichander et al., 2022 ; She et al., 2023 ; Tafjord et al., 2021 ; Sinha et al., 2019 ; Trivedi et al., 2022 ; Kuratov et al., 2024 ; Larson et al., 2019 ; FitzGerald et al., 2023 ; Jin et al., 2023 ; Kazemi et al., 2023 ) . These records have no paired probes. They allow boundaries in general reading to be compared with boundaries in agent decisions; this paper does not analyze them and does not use them as a measure of next-action skill.

sections.heading: C.4 Splits, freezing and audits
sections.text: Records are split into dev and test by a hash of their source group (game, user, repository), so no source contributes to both splits. Dev is used for template and pipeline checks and for selecting the reasoning reference, and is always reported separately from test. The target is 300 test records per difficulty cell, sampled with matched pairs across cells where a ladder requires them. The full population, including every request byte, option order and label, is frozen in a hash-sealed manifest before analysis, and all systems receive the identical requests. An independent content audit found 42 test records with conflicting labels outside the control groups and 56 test records whose inputs also occur in dev. We keep the frozen population unchanged and report a sensitivity analysis that excludes these 98 records. Public training games cannot be assumed unseen by pretrained models, which is one reason we add freshly generated confirmation cohorts. Fixed public items can also be overfit. The generators we use for the follow-up studies, including one for decision states whose probes are sufficient by construction (§ 6.1 ), can draw new evaluation states at any time.

sections.heading: Systems.
sections.text: Table 1 lists the seventeen fast systems and the reasoning reference, grouped by type. Fourteen are System One models, which return a native distribution over the supplied options in one pass. Two are hosted APIs: JEV and OpenAI Decisions ( OpenAI, 2026a ) . Ten are released open-weight models that we serve locally, pinned to released revisions, each with its authors’ own serving code and documented settings: Clef-27B, Kev-9B, CLM-8B, Laya, Eikos-27B, Perplexity Decider-27B, SimpleJev-27B, Vega-27B, Torchcast-27B and Quyet-1.0-Large. Two are published recipes that read a frozen open-weight language model through the same interface: Cygnet reads masked single-letter probabilities of Gemma-4-12B, scores long option lists in groups of 20 and calibrates the result, and Decider-chat-31B reads the answer-letter distribution of Gemma-4-31B-it with a temperature that depends on the number of options. The three open-weight language models are scored by complete-option likelihood with thinking disabled. We render the state, question and enumerated options with the model’s chat template, sum the log probabilities of each option’s full name followed by the end-of-turn token, and normalize over the options. This exposes a full distribution that is directly comparable in form to those of the System One models. A hosted reasoning model (GPT-6.1 Sol, medium reasoning) answers each question in a separate call with the selected option and a verbalized distribution. It serves as a reference with deliberation, not as a competitor to the System One models; it answered all 174,513 questions of the benchmark (322 answers could not be parsed and count as wrong). Further released System One models are being evaluated with the same client, request format and run records; we report only systems for which every record and every condition is complete.

sections.heading: Identical inputs.
sections.text: Every system receives the same frozen request: the same state, question text, options, descriptions and option order. We never truncate a state, drop options or reselect records to fit a system. When a request exceeds a system’s documented input limit, the question is recorded as unsupported, counted wrong, and reported as coverage. This affects Laya (512 input tokens, and option lists longer than its 192-token head budget), Cygnet (726 records over its 16k context) and Gemma (4 records over 32k). It also affects Quyet-1.0-Large, whose runtime refuses questions with more than ten options, which includes every ALFWorld decision: only 3.8% of paired test states have all of its answers supported. Perplexity Decider-27B refuses questions whose prompt exceeds 8,192 tokens (9.3% of paired states have a refused answer, mostly in τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench and the visible-field probes); Decider-chat-31B and OpenAI Decisions refuse 0.3–0.4%. Vega-27B’s server runs out of memory on the longest states on one 80 GB H100; after three failures on a healthy server we record such a question as unsupported (9,237 answers; 5.0% of paired states), and SimpleJev-27B’s server fails repeatedly on the longest states (13,119 answers recorded as unsupported after the same rules; 6.6% of paired states). Two author runtimes shorten long states themselves before reading them (Table 1 ); we report them as shipped. Readouts differ across systems by design, so comparisons are between deployed choice interfaces. They do not isolate the effect of architecture, model size or training data. Where an analysis uses a subset of questions, a system that answers fewer than half of them is left out of that analysis and named (the coverage rule ).

sections.heading: What is evaluated.
sections.text: All seventeen fast systems and the reasoning reference receive all 65,228 records, including every paired test state. The trace-ablation condition was run for all seventeen fast systems on the 10,897 original agent records that carry it. Closed-loop execution, in which a System One model acts as the policy in a live environment, is outside the scope of this paper’s results.

sections.heading: Latency.
sections.text: Accuracy runs batch requests for throughput, so their timings are not latency. We therefore time a separate fixed latency panel of 163 test items, one per main difficulty cell, so that every group, context length (37 to 99k characters), question count (1–8) and option count (2–255) is represented. Each system answers all questions of an item in one request, strictly sequentially, after five untimed warm-up items. We run three passes in reshuffled order and report the first pass, excluding the warm-up items; repeated passes, which benefit from caches, are reported separately. Only complete answers count toward latency, and refusals are reported as coverage. For pairs of systems we also report the median of per-request time ratios on the requests both answer, which is more robust than a ratio of medians. Seven systems, marked in Table 1 , were not timed on this panel. Their accuracy runs, unlike those of the other systems, send one request at a time to a server on its own H100 (or, for OpenAI Decisions, to the hosted API), so we estimate their latency from those runs on the same 158 timed panel items; these estimates lack the panel’s warm-up and are marked separately in Figure 2 . The reasoning reference answers one question per request, so we time it through its synchronous API on the same panel and order, sending the questions of an item in parallel; all 158 timed items were answered, with a median of 2.3 s per item, about eleven times JEV’s.

sections.heading: Cost.
sections.text: System One models emphasize intelligence per dollar, so we report cost next to accuracy (Figure 2 ). The hosted JEV model was billed for 209.2M input tokens over all 65,228 records, $8.79 in total or $0.13 per 1,000 decision states. For self-hosted systems we estimate cost from the panel’s time per state at a stated GPU price; all were timed on the same hardware class, one request at a time (for the self-hosted systems not timed on it, from their accuracy runs; § D ). On these estimates the efficient frontier runs from Laya and Kev-9B through Cygnet, Decider-chat-31B and JEV to Eikos-27B and Gemma-4-31B. Eikos-27B reaches 0.795 at an estimated $0.19 per 1,000 states, about 1.4 times JEV’s measured cost, and displaces Clef-27B from the frontier; moving from JEV to Gemma raises paired decision accuracy from 0.763 to 0.811 at about five times the cost per state, while the Qwen readouts and CLM are dominated. The second hosted decision model, OpenAI Decisions, was billed for 186.9M input tokens on the 65,228 records ($18.69 at $0.10 per million input tokens, output free), $0.29 per 1,000 decision states or about twice JEV’s cost, for a paired decision accuracy of 0.706. The reasoning reference is shown for orientation only: its full run cost $642.00 under batch pricing, $9.84 per 1,000 decision states or about 73 times JEV, for a paired decision accuracy of 0.884 (§ 5.1 ).

sections.heading: Model versions and reproducibility.
sections.text: Open models are pinned to released revisions and served with recorded configurations. JEV is pinned by its version string ( jev-1.13.0 ), but its provider does not promise long-term support for a version, and hosted serving can change or fail: during one check on 5 October 2026, 16 of 24 minimal requests returned server errors. We therefore re-ran the decision question alone on a stratified sample (up to 25 per cell) of 2,783 paired test states on 6 October, after the formal runs had finished on 1 October. The selected action matched the formal run on 96.3% of states (2,681/2,783). Because the formal requests also carried the probe questions, this agreement bounds the combined effect of version drift, serving nondeterminism and request packing; it does not isolate any one of them. OpenAI Decisions is a public beta identified only by its model name ( gpt-6-luna ); all of its records were collected on 11 October 2026. We keep all raw requests, full output distributions and timestamps, so that later versions can be compared on identical inputs.

sections.heading: Appendix F Decision-oriented probes: definitions
sections.text: All probe answers are derived from the task sentence, the initial observation and the trace. For each state we ask: the agent’s location (all receptacles plus “the middle of the room”); what it holds (all objects seen plus “nothing”); for every object type the task still needs, where an instance was last seen that is still available (all receptacles plus “not seen yet”); whether the held target object has already been cleaned, heated or cooled; how many target objects are already in place (two-object tasks); for every receptacle, whether the agent has gone there; and the next sub-goal. Sub-goal categories are defined by mapping each admissible action through the parsed state: search (an unvisited receptacle), fetch (a receptacle where a needed object was seen), open the receptacle here, take a needed object, go to the appliance, process, go to the destination, place, use the lamp, and two residual categories (another object; look, examine or inventory). The gold sub-goal is the set of categories of the gold actions. States whose gold actions fall into a residual category or into a revisit of a searched receptacle were excluded; all inspected cases were co-located receptacles (Appendix E ). Of 705 sampled ALFWorld states, 644 remain. The probe request contains 26 questions per state on average.

sections.heading: Appendix G Generated procedures
sections.text: The generator produces states in a household domain (a home robot following a house protocol) and an orders domain (a support agent following a refund policy). Each procedure is a decision list over four rule facts with a default action; the trace establishes eight binary facts (the four rule facts and four distractors) through observations, some of which are later overwritten. The action set is fixed per domain and includes actions licensed by the distractor facts, so a model that acts on any true fact can be wrong. Sufficiency (a unique gold action for every assignment of the four rule facts) is verified by enumeration. Dev seeds were used only for template checks; the 1,200 test states use disjoint seeds.

This makes them fast and cheap, but when they choose wrongly there is nothing to inspect: did the model misread what the agent has seen, or read it correctly and still act wrongly? We answer behaviorally. On a frozen benchmark of agent decision states from simulated environments, customer-service policies, tool use, web navigation and coding, we pair every next-action question with factual probes about the same state, each answered independently. Across seventeen fast systems and a reasoning model, the answer is consistent: most wrong actions follow correct reading, and the more accurate a system, the more of its errors take this form. These errors are not noise; they gather on the same states across systems of every kind. Where the probed facts provably determine the action, models that read every fact still fail to combine them, and their own answers, composed by code, repair the failure. On real states, what is missing is often not a fact but the next sub-goal. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Paired measurement on a real ALFWorld state. Left: the goal, the history and all 31 admissible actions; the gold action follows only from what the trace reveals. Middle: the decision and each factual probe are answered independently on the same state (JEV’s answers: every probe right, action wrong). Right: crossing all facts correct ( U U ) with action correct ( D D ) gives four outcomes; this state is facts right, action wrong. An agent acting in an environment repeatedly reads the feedback of its previous actions, works out where it stands, and chooses what to do next. In most current agents each such step is a call to a large language model that writes out its reasoning and then names an action ( Yao et al., 2023 ) . A growing family of System One models takes a different route ( TypeSafe AI, 2026 ; Liquid AI, 2026 ; Kwok et al., 2026 ; Palmer, 2026 ; Convai Innovations, 2026 ; Cloudflare, 2026 ) . Given the agent’s state and a set of candidate answers, they return a probability distribution over the supplied options and generate no text; their output is consumed directly by code, and their developers emphasize intelligence per dollar ( TypeSafe AI, 2026 ) . The System One models we evaluate answer a complete state in a median of 27–225 ms, against 317–947 ms for likelihood readouts of open-weight language models and 2.3 s for a reasoning model (§ 4 ). We study only their choice interface , in which the model selects among supplied options. When such a model picks the wrong action, there is no chain of thought to read. The error has two very different explanations. The model may have misread what the agent already knows, for example by missing that the last action failed or losing track of what it holds; or it may have read all of it correctly and still chosen badly . The first points to the state representation or the context budget, the second to the decision itself. Final-action accuracy cannot tell these cases apart, and generated rationales need not reflect the computation behind an answer ( Turpin et al., 2023 ; Lanham et al., 2023 ) . Conversely, a correct action does not show that the model understood the trace. We therefore ask, behaviorally: can System One models understand the information an agent has obtained and act correctly on it, and when they fail, can we tell failures of comprehension from failures of decision? On a single agent decision state we ask, each in isolation, the next-action question and factual probes whose answers the environment determines, such as whether the last action succeeded, what the agent carries, or whether an action is permitted. Crossing “all measured facts correct” with “action correct” gives four observable outcomes (Figure 1 ). Around this measurement we build a frozen benchmark of 65,228 records, 19,663 of them paired test states, from simulators with exact ground truth (ALFWorld, BabyAI-Text, TextWorld), customer-service policies ( τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench), tool use, web navigation and coding traces, with every admissible action in context and gold labels computed only from what the agent has seen. We evaluate seventeen fast systems, fourteen System One models of three kinds (hosted APIs, open-weight models, and recipes that read a frozen language model) and three likelihood readouts of open-weight language models, with a reasoning model, GPT-6.1, as a reference. The short answer is that these models mostly read right and act wrong. Our main findings are: • Most wrong actions follow correct reading. For the six most accurate systems, 73–85% of decision errors occur on states where every measured fact is answered correctly, and the share grows with accuracy (§ 5.1 ). • The errors are structured. All 14 competent fast systems fail with every fact right on the same 141 states, where chance predicts none (§ 5.3 ). • When the probes suffice, the failure is composition. On generated states whose probes determine the action, models that read every fact and decide perfectly from the facts alone lose 20–45 points when they must do both from the trace. Their own fact answers recover 15–28 points, and composing the action in code from them reaches 0.96–1.00 (§ 6.1 ). • On real states, the decision itself is often missing. Correct answers to the benchmark’s probes add at most 7 points for all but two systems. On ALFWorld, stating the next sub-goal adds 16 points for JEV, any block of facts at most 5 (§ 6.2 , § 6.3 ). • Accuracy hides the rest. Removing the history collapses accuracy where earlier observations matter, policy edits are read correctly but acted on in only 22–72% of cases, and calibration error ranges from 2.6% to 26.6% (§ 7 ). We also contribute a model-free criterion for when probes can support attributing an error to the decision (§ 2.4 ), states that satisfy it by construction, and an evaluation of eighteen systems that combines the paired diagnostics with cost, latency and calibration. The paired outcomes are behavioral evidence: they do not identify a model’s internal computation, and we do not claim that the probes exhaust every relevant fact. 2 Measuring Comprehension and Decision on the Same State 2.1 Decision states A decision state s s consists of a task goal, the executed history of actions and the observations they produced, any rules that govern the environment or policy, and the set 𝒜 ⁡ ( s ) \mathcal{A}(s) of admissible next actions. The model must choose one element of 𝒜 ⁡ ( s ) \mathcal{A}(s) and is never asked to generate an action. Every admissible action is placed in context with its name and a description, nothing is shortlisted, and no language model proposes candidates; tool calls with open arguments are enumerated from the environment or database. Gold is a set G ⁡ ( s ) ⊆ 𝒜 ⁡ ( s ) G(s)\subseteq\mathcal{A}(s) computed only from information available to the agent: in the simulators, the first actions of all shortest plans on a map built from what the trace entails, or, when the needed objects have not yet been seen, the actions that reveal unseen locations. A decision is correct, D ⁡ ( s ) = 1 D(s)=1 , if the chosen action lies in G ⁡ ( s ) G(s) . 2.2 Factual probes On annotated states we also ask closed factual probes whose answers the simulator state, database or data labels determine: the outcome of the last action, the agent’s location and inventory, completed subgoals, whether an action is permitted, and which observation establishes a fact. Each question, probe or decision, is answered on the state alone; several may share a request, but no question or answer is added to another question’s input and no gold fact is revealed. “Paired” means that the input state is identical, not that we observe stages of the model’s computation. 2.3 Four observable outcomes Let U i = 1 U_{i}=1 if all applicable probes of state i i are answered correctly. U i U_{i} is measured-fact performance, not complete understanding. Crossing U U with D D gives four outcomes; we write U1D0 for U = 1 , D = 0 U{=}1,D{=}0 (facts right, action wrong), and U1D1, U0D1, U0D0 likewise. Each licenses less than it may seem (Table 5 in Appendix B ); in particular, U1D0 does not show that the failure lies purely in deciding, and U0D1 does not show a shortcut. Questions a system cannot answer because of an input limit are counted wrong and reported as coverage. We report counts pooled over the 19,663 paired test states, which summarize prevalence and are not a ranking statistic (cell-weighted estimates and cluster bootstrap: Appendix B.3 ). 2.4 When can a probe set support the diagnosis? A U1D0 outcome suggests a decision failure only if the probes capture what the decision requires, and this can be checked without the model. Holding goal, rules and remaining context fixed, let P ⁡ ( s ) P(s) be the vector of correct probe answers. For a group of states S S sharing a probe vector, the probe set is sufficient on S S if ⋂ s ∈ S G ⁡ ( s ) ≠ ∅ , \textstyle\bigcap_{s\in S}G(s)\neq\emptyset, (1) that is, if some action is correct in every state the agent could be in given those answers. If two states share the correct probe answers but have disjoint gold sets, answering every probe correctly cannot determine the action, and a wrong action after correct probes cannot be attributed to deciding alone. Pairwise intersections are not enough; the check must consider the whole group. In finite environments it is exhaustive; in natural data, absence of a counterexample does not prove sufficiency. Passing it means the probes can support a diagnosis, not that the model uses those facts. 2.5 Controlled variations To see what drives the outcomes, the benchmark also contains a trace ablation that removes the executed history, observation minimal pairs that edit only the last observation relevantly or irrelevantly, stated rule changes that make prior knowledge wrong, and difficulty ladders over trace length and the distance from the decisive observation (§ 7 ); encoding controls are not analyzed here (Appendix B.5 ). 3 Benchmark The frozen benchmark has 65,228 records, 59,234 test and 5,994 dev (Table 6 in Appendix C ). Most paired states come from three simulators with exact ground truth: ALFWorld, BabyAI-Text and TextWorld cooking games ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ; Paglieri et al., 2025 ; Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2019 ; Carta et al., 2023 ; Côté et al., 2018 ; Cui et al., 2025 ) . Trajectories are rolled out by each environment’s expert, by a noisy variant and by a variant that issues invalid commands, so traces contain failures and detours; no language model takes part. Gold sets were checked against breadth-first search in the real environments. From τ 2 \tau^{2} -bench airline and retail ( Barres et al., 2026 ) we take policy-constrained states with tool calls enumerated from the database and probes on record fields and permissions. Tool selection, web navigation and AgentRM trees ( Xu et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2025 ; Patil et al., 2025 ; Ross et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2023 ; Xia et al., 2025 ) carry probes on fields stated in the trace (the visible-field probes), and 360 coding records built from real repository histories ask which edit caused a regression and which limited next action follows. Ladders vary trace length, distance from the decisive observation and novelty, and confirmation cohorts generated later from new seeds re-test the findings on states no earlier run had seen. A further 32,700 records of text-understanding primitives are part of the frozen population but not analyzed here. A facts-right, action-wrong outcome may also come from a wrong label. Two audits bound this. An independent content audit found 42 test records with conflicting labels and 56 whose inputs also occur in dev; excluding these 98 records changes no group score of any of the eighteen systems by more than 3.5 points (§ C.4 ). Second, while building the decision-oriented probes of § 6.3 we re-derived every ALFWorld label from the text of the trace alone. In the original ALFWorld cohorts, several receptacles can share one simulator location, and the builder recorded only one of them. For 303 paired test records, the location label therefore names a co-located receptacle rather than the one the text says the agent arrived at, and the four strong systems we audited answer the receptacle named in the text (98–99%), so these records cannot reach U = 1 U{=}1 (Appendix E ). A facts-right, action-wrong outcome on a natural state has two readings. The probes may have missed a decision-relevant fact (§ 2.4 ), or the model may have read everything it needed and still not combined it into the right action. On natural states the two cannot be separated, so we first build states where they can, and then return to real benchmark states. Figure 7 summarizes the three studies. We generate decision states in two domains, a household text world and a customer service policy. Each state has a goal, a numbered decision list of four rules followed by a default action (“apply the first rule whose condition holds”), an executed trace that establishes eight binary facts, and a fixed set of nine actions. Four of the facts are tested by the rules; the other four are distractors, each tied to a plausible action outside the procedure, and any fact may be established and then overwritten by later feedback. The ladder variable is the position of the first rule whose condition holds (1–4, or none, so that the default applies). Later rules hold independently with probability 0.5, so that choosing a later rule whose condition also holds (a precedence error) can be told apart from choosing a rule whose condition does not hold. For every assignment of the four rule facts the gold action is unique, which we verify by enumeration. The probes ask the four rule facts and two of the distractors, so correct answers to the rule-fact probes determine the action, and U = 1 , D = 0 U{=}1,D{=}0 can only be a failure to use facts that were read. On the same 1,200 test states (120 per domain and ladder position) we ask the decision under four inputs: the raw trace; the trace plus the current values of the four rule facts; the trace plus the current values of the four distractor facts, in the same form (a control for added text); and the values of all eight facts without the trace. On 644 ALFWorld states we derive, from the text of the trace alone, everything a planner would need: the agent’s location and inventory, where each still-needed object was last seen, whether the held object has been cleaned, heated or cooled, how many objects are already in place, which receptacles have not yet been visited, and the next sub-goal (search, fetch, take, go to the appliance, process, go to the destination, place, use the lamp). We validate the parse against the simulator labels (§ 5.4 ) and ask each fact as a narrow, independent question, about 26 per state. We then add to the decision request either the decision-oriented facts, a complete digest of the observed state, the next sub-goal, or facts plus sub-goal, each with correct values, and the same blocks filled with each system’s own answers (Table 4 , Figure 9 b). The facts are read; the sub-goal is not chosen. JEV answers the narrow probes almost perfectly: 99.7% of the 14,104 visited-or-not questions, 100% for the held object and placed count, 96.9% for where needed objects were seen. Yet decision-oriented facts add only 5.3 points, no more than the benchmark’s own probes (5.7), and a complete state digest adds 4.7. Stating the next sub-goal adds 16.3 points, and facts plus sub-goal 21.3, reaching 0.929. JEV’s own answer to the sub-goal question is right in only 66.8% of states, so the same block filled with its own answers adds 6.4. Of JEV’s 183 errors when deciding alone, 41% have every fact right but the sub-goal wrong, and another 37% have both right when asked separately: JEV can state the sub-goal it then fails to pursue. For JEV, the remaining errors on real ALFWorld states are errors of planning, not of reading or of consolidation. Stronger systems are limited elsewhere. The same blocks help Clef, Gemma and Qwen3.8-27B much less: no block adds more than 10 points, and the sub-goal adds about 6. Their own answers help only Qwen3.8-27B (+4.8 with facts, +6.2 with facts and sub-goal); for Clef and Gemma they change nothing ( − 1.2 -1.2 to + 0.3 +0.3 ). GPT-6.1 decides alone at 0.953 and no block, correct or its own, adds more than 2.5 points. How well a system answers the sub-goal question does not predict whether its answers help. Clef answers it best (89.1%) and gains nothing; of Clef’s errors when deciding alone, nearly half (48%) occur with every fact and the sub-goal answered correctly in separate requests. Qwen3.8-27B answers it worst (36.0%, below its own decision accuracy) and still gains, through the facts; GPT-6.1 answers it equally poorly (35.2%) while deciding correctly in 95% of states, so its decisions do not pass through the sub-goal as the benchmark labels it. The decision-oriented facts can even hurt: on states where one needed object has been seen and another has not, listing the unvisited receptacles sends Gemma and Qwen3.8-27B to search instead of fetching what they already know about, and Gemma’s accuracy on these states falls from 0.659 to 0.341. With every block given, most of Gemma’s remaining errors pick the right kind of action for the wrong object. Extra information is not neutral: a salient but incomplete summary can pull a model away from the trace it otherwise reads well. The other systems. The seven other System One models that answer ALFWorld decisions confirm that the sub-goal is the most useful single block: it adds 6.7–13.8 points for six of them (OpenAI Decisions +11.0, CI [+7.2, +14.9]; Eikos-27B +13.8), while decision-oriented facts add 0.9–3.3 points, except for Vega-27B (+5.0) and Eikos-27B (+8.9), which gains 18.5 from facts plus sub-goal. Like Clef and Gemma rather than JEV, the others mostly answer the sub-goal question well (0.77–0.87; SimpleJev-27B 0.64), and 32–64% of their errors when deciding alone occur with every fact and the sub-goal answered correctly in separate requests. Their own answers help less than the correct ones, and OpenAI Decisions’ own facts and sub-goal even lower its accuracy ( − 2.6 -2.6 , CI [ − 7.1 -7.1 , + 1.9 +1.9 ]). The pull of an incomplete summary also recurs: on the states where one needed object has been seen and another has not, correct decision facts lower OpenAI Decisions from 0.698 to 0.543 and Decider-chat-31B from 0.698 to 0.434, although Vega-27B and Torchcast-27B gain on the same states (0.713 to 0.806 and 0.302 to 0.496). What this means. Across these studies, the source of a facts-right, action-wrong error varies by system and by state: consolidation of scattered evidence for JEV and Qwen3.8-27B on rule procedures, capture by irrelevant cues for Clef, sub-goal selection for JEV on household tasks, and grounding a sub-goal in the right object for Gemma. Each calls for a different remedy, and only the paired measurement, combined with probes that are sufficient for the decision, reveals which applies. 7 Controls, Boundaries and Calibration The paired outcomes describe single states. When a single observation is edited so that the gold action changes (Figure 10 c), Cygnet, Clef and Gemma change their decision in 91–96% of ALFWorld triples, Qwen3.8-27B in 79% and JEV in 71%, while all keep their decision after an irrelevant edit in 89–97% of cases. Scoring a supplied set of answers, long used in classification and reranking, is now offered as a programmable interface for agents, by hosted models ( TypeSafe AI, 2026 ; OpenAI, 2026a ; Liquid AI, 2026 ) and open alternatives ( Kwok et al., 2026 ; Palmer, 2026 ; Cloudflare, 2026 ; Convai Innovations, 2026 ; Vicentino, 2026 ; Perplexity AI, 2026 ; SimpleJev, 2026 ; vLLM Semantic Router Team, 2026 ; Nguyen, 2026 ; Blockbrain Labs, 2026 ; Mapika, 2026 ) . As an evaluation judge, JEV approaches a reasoning judge where a verdict can be read off the text but falls behind where it must be derived, and its confidence can decide when to escalate ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Public comparisons report aggregate scores ( Apolinário, 2026 ) ; agent benchmarks measure task success, progress or per-step correctness ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ; Ma et al., 2024 ; Barres et al., 2026 ; Deng et al., 2023 ) , and fixed histories with a next-action question are established ( George et al., 2024 ) . We ask what such accuracy leaves unexplained, pairing each decision with probes on the same state. Knowing versus doing, and composition. Studies of agents ( Schmied et al., 2026 ; Sobotka et al., 2026 ; Deb and Krishnan, 2026 ; Arghal et al., 2026 ) separate what an agent appears to know from what it does. Language models are also distracted by irrelevant context ( Shi et al., 2023 ) , plan better with an external component ( Valmeekam et al., 2023 ; Kambhampati et al., 2024 ) , and answer every sub-question of a problem yet fail the composed question ( Press et al., 2023 ) . Our setting exposes neither text nor hidden states, the probes are answered in isolation on the exact state, and we test whether the probe set can support the diagnosis at all. The remedies we test mirror decomposed and program-aided reasoning ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; Khot et al., 2023 ; Gao et al., 2023 ) , but the sub-questions go to the same choice-only model and the composition is done by the calling program. Behavioral diagnosis. Chains of thought need not be faithful to the computation behind an answer ( Turpin et al., 2023 ; Lanham et al., 2023 ) . Like behavioral testing ( Ribeiro et al., 2020 ) , and unlike probing classifiers ( Belinkov, 2022 ) , we infer competence from controlled questions and input variations. Appendix A discusses each line of work, cost-aware routing and failure attribution in full. 9 Discussion What a practitioner can do. The results suggest a simple procedure for deploying a System One model in an agent loop. First, measure the paired outcomes on the target states. If most errors follow misread facts, the remedy lies in the state representation, the trace format or the context budget. If most follow correct reading, as for every strong system here, the next question is whether the decision-relevant facts are known and the rules explicit. Where they are, as on our generated procedures, the strongest remedy is to ask the facts as narrow parallel questions and compose the action in code, which brought every system we tried to 0.96–1.00 at the price of a second batch of cheap questions; a confidence cascade keeps most of the gain with a second request on a third of the states. Where the decision requires choosing a sub-goal in an open task, as in ALFWorld, appending facts helps little, and the missing ingredient is a sub-goal that the model does not reliably supply; that is a planning problem, for a planner, for training, or for a deliberating model on the few states that need it. A diagnostic instrument, not a leaderboard. The pooled accuracies of Table 2 hide most of what matters. Rankings change across domains (Figure 4 ); a perfect action score on coding traces hides a twelve-point difference in reading; two systems with similar paired accuracy fail for different reasons (consolidation for JEV, cue capture for Clef); and the most accurate fast system, Gemma’s likelihood readout, is among the least calibrated. Fast decision models are therefore better evaluated with diagnostic panels and their controls, and with freshly generated states whose probes are sufficient by construction, that match the kind of state a workflow depends on, than with a single number. Fast is not the same as cheap to trust. GPT-6.1 shows what deliberation buys on the same states: seven to twelve points of decision accuracy at roughly seventy times the cost of JEV. It does not change the kind of error that remains. For agent builders, the interesting design space is therefore not System One versus reasoning models, but which states a fast model can be trusted on, which need a composed decision, and which need deliberation. The paired measurement, the probe-sufficiency check and the model’s own calibration are the instruments for drawing that line. 10 Limitations Behavioral evidence only. The paired outcomes are observations on identical inputs. They do not show which internal computation produced an action, and a correct probe answer does not prove that the model used that fact. Probe coverage. On natural states the probes are not sufficient for the decision, so a facts-right, action-wrong outcome mixes decision failures with facts we did not ask about; the generated ladder and the decision-oriented probes address this only for the domains they cover. Labels. Gold actions are computed from agent-observable information, but they can be stricter than necessary (5–42% of a system’s simulator errors are in fact optimal) and, in the original ALFWorld cohorts, co-located receptacles produce wrong location labels for 303 of 8,197 paired ALFWorld records; we keep the frozen labels and report sensitivity analyses. Deployments, not architectures. Systems differ in serving stack, readout and input limits, two author runtimes shorten long states themselves, and hosted models can change between versions (96.3% agreement on a JEV rerun after five days; OpenAI Decisions is a public beta). Scope. We evaluate single decisions on frozen traces, not closed-loop execution, and the follow-up studies of § 6 cover a subset of systems: the composition ladder and probe-then-decide sixteen each, and the decision-oriented probes twelve (each count includes the reasoning reference). The reasoning reference answered each question in a separate call with a verbalized distribution, so its calibration is not comparable. 11 Conclusion A fast decision model that errs leaves nothing behind but a wrong action. By asking the same model, on the same state, what it read and what it chose, we find that for strong systems the problem is usually not reading. Across seventeen fast systems and a reasoning model, most wrong actions follow correct reading, and they gather on states that defeat systems of every kind. Reading right and acting wrong is therefore not the mark of weak models but the characteristic failure of strong ones. Nor is it a single failure. When the decisive facts are known, models fail to combine them, and their own answers, composed by code, repair the decision; in open tasks they lack the next sub-goal, which additional facts do not supply. Both point to one way of building agents on fast models: let the model read, through many narrow questions, and hand the composition of the decision to code, to a planner, or to deliberation where a state requires it. Measuring reading and acting separately is what tells which a state requires. References Apolinário (2026) Apolinário Jev Decision Index .
